newsitem.title: PAPUA NEW GUINEA: British mercenary leader free to leave PNG.
newsitem.headline: British mercenary leader free to leave PNG.

text.p: British colonel Tim Spicer, detained in Papua New Guinea for more than three weeks after an aborted mercenary operation, was told on Tuesday he was free to leave after illegal firearm charges against him were dropped.

"I am greatly relieved. Now I can go home," said a tired looking Spicer after he completed giving evidence at an inquiry into his mission which saw the South Pacific nation's army rebel and force the prime minister Sir Julius Chan to step aside.
The only obstacle facing Spicer was the fact that Port Moresby's Boroko District Court had lost his passport, his lawyer said.
Spicer, a 44-year-old former Scots Guard, had pleaded not guilty to illegally possessing a Russian Makarov pistol and 40 rounds of ammunition.
But the charges were dropped on Monday evening because of legal problems with the way his Port Moresby flat was searched and the pistol seized.
"On the advice of the public prosecutor the charges were dropped," Chief of Police Prosecution Wee Kati told Reuters just before the scheduled start of Spicer's trial.
Spicer's US$36 million mission to end the nine-year secessionist rebellion on Bougainville island sparked the worst political crisis in Papua New Guinea since independence in 1975.

Spicer was detained by rebel army officers on March 16 and his 70 African soldiers kicked out, leaving behind a country scared from two days of looting and violence as pro-army supporters rallied against the prime minister and mercenaries.

Spicer was eventually handed over to police to be charged with illegally possessing a firearm and ammunition. On March 24, he pleaded not guilty and was ordered by the court to stay in the British High Commissioner's residence until his trial.

Spicer, whose service with the British army included a spell as a senior U.N. peacekeeper in Bosnia, claimed his contract with the PNG government sanctioned him and his foreign soldiers as "special police constables" with the right to carry weapons.
A manifest of weapons in the contract, included not only two Russian-made helicopter gunships, but also 20 Makarov pistols.
Political analysts in Papua New Guinea suggested at the time that the charges were a pretext to keep Spicer in the country in order for him to testify at the mercenary inquiry.
Inquiry head Judge Warwick Andrew on Tuesday thanked Spicer for his cooperation and told him he was free to return home to London, but added he may be recalled to give further evidence.
"The inquiry has had a job to do and I am glad my part in it is over," Spicer said as he walked away from the inquiry, which is due to end on April 18.

In his three and a half days in the witness box, Spicer detailed how his mercenary plan was hatched in clandestine meetings, starting in a coffee shop in the Australian resort town of Cairns in 1996 and then Hong Kong and London.
Spicer also supported his company Sandline International, a British-based military consultancy, and its mission as a valid business venture with the PNG government.

He also denied he was seeking mining concessions on Bougainville, despite a Sandline document with his signature suggesting a joint venture with the government to run Bougavnille's giant Panguna copper mine once recaptured.

Executive Outcomes, which supplied Sandline with the mercenaries, is Africa's best known private army having operated in Angola and Sierre Leone. It is believed to have been paid for some of its operations with shares in mining concessions.
In an Australian radio interview on Tuesday, Spicer said his mission was to improve the PNG defence force's capability to boost the government's hand in peace negotiations.
Spicer said that simply having the firepower did not mean it would be used. "Sometimes it's enough to have them (weapons) and to threaten to use them without actually using them," he said.
